title.en: Section 1 - Phone Call about Library Membership
title.zh: 第一部分 - 关于图书馆会员的电话

sections.passage: A phone call between a new resident, Andrew, and a librarian at the Westfield Public Library. Andrew has recently moved to the area and wants to join the library. The librarian, Helen, explains the membership options. There are three types of membership: standard, premium, and family. The standard membership costs 25 pounds per year and allows members to borrow up to six books at a time for a three-week period. The premium membership costs 45 pounds per year and includes borrowing privileges for up to twelve items including books, DVDs, and audiobooks, with a four-week loan period. The family membership costs 60 pounds per year and covers up to four family members, with a combined borrowing limit of twenty items. Andrew mentions that he has a wife and two teenage children, so Helen recommends the family membership. Helen also explains that the library has a digital lending service where members can borrow e-books and audiobooks through an app called Libby, which is included with all membership types at no extra charge. Andrew asks about late return fees, and Helen tells him that items returned after the due date incur a fine of 20 pence per item per day, with a maximum fine of 5 pounds per item. Lost or damaged items must be replaced at the current retail price. Helen also mentions that the library hosts several free events including a weekly book club on Wednesday evenings, a children's story time session on Saturday mornings, and monthly author talks. Andrew signs up for the family membership and pays by debit card.

title.en: Section 2 - Guided Tour of a Museum
title.zh: 第二部分 - 博物馆导览

sections.passage: Welcome to the Greenfield Museum of Natural History. My name is Robert, and I'll be your guide for today's tour. Before we begin, let me give you some practical information. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 AM to 5 PM, with the last admission at 4:15 PM. We are closed on Mondays except during school holidays. Today's tour will last approximately ninety minutes and will cover three of our most popular galleries. We'll start in the Earth Sciences Gallery on the ground floor, which houses our impressive collection of minerals, fossils, and geological specimens. The highlight of this gallery is a complete skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus Rex, which was discovered in Montana in 1998 and measures over twelve metres in length. From there, we'll move to the Marine Life Gallery on the first floor, where you can see our aquarium featuring over fifty species of tropical fish, as well as displays on ocean conservation and the impact of plastic pollution on marine ecosystems. The gallery includes a touch pool where children can handle starfish, sea urchins, and hermit crabs under supervision. Our final stop will be the Human Origins Gallery on the second floor, which traces the evolution of humans from our earliest ancestors to modern Homo sapiens. This gallery features several interactive displays and a replica of the Lascaux cave paintings from France. After the tour, you're welcome to visit the museum cafe on the ground floor, which serves hot and cold food and has a lovely view of the botanical garden. I should also mention that the museum gift shop, located near the main entrance, stocks a wide range of books, educational toys, and souvenirs. Please note that photography is allowed in all galleries without flash, and we ask that you do not touch any exhibits unless specifically indicated. If you have any questions during the tour, please don't hesitate to ask.

title.en: Section 3 - Students Planning a Community Project
title.zh: 第三部分 - 学生规划社区项目

sections.passage: Three students, Lisa, Omar, and Kate, are meeting in the university library to discuss their Community Engagement project. They need to plan and execute a project that benefits the local community as part of their final-year assessment. Lisa has done some preliminary research and suggests three possible projects: organizing a community garden, running a series of health awareness workshops, or setting up a homework tutoring programme for local school children. After discussing the options, the group decides to go with the community garden project because it addresses multiple community needs including food security, environmental education, and social cohesion. Omar proposes locating the garden on the disused land behind the community centre on Elm Street. He has already spoken to the community centre manager, Mrs. Fernandez, who is enthusiastic about the idea and has offered to let them use the land free of charge. Kate volunteers to handle the budget and fundraising. She estimates they will need approximately 800 pounds for materials including raised beds, soil, seeds, tools, and a small storage shed. She plans to apply for a grant from the university's Community Fund, which provides up to 500 pounds for student-led community projects, and approach local businesses for additional sponsorship. Lisa will coordinate the volunteer recruitment drive, aiming to get at least twenty local residents involved. They agree to hold an initial planning meeting with community members on Saturday the 15th of March at 2 PM at the community centre. The project timeline spans twelve weeks, with the first four weeks dedicated to site preparation and planting, followed by eight weeks of maintenance and growth. They plan to harvest the first crops in late June and organize a community celebration event. Omar will create a project website and social media pages to document progress and attract more volunteers. Each student will keep a reflective journal throughout the project, which will form part of their assessment portfolio. They agree to meet weekly on Thursdays at 4 PM to review progress and address any issues.

title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于睡眠科学的讲座

sections.passage:
Good afternoon. Today's lecture in our series on Health and Wellbeing focuses on the science of sleep, a topic that has attracted increasing attention from researchers in recent decades. Despite spending approximately one-third of our lives asleep, we are only now beginning to fully understand the complex biological processes that occur during sleep and the profound effects that sleep deprivation has on human health and cognitive function. Sleep is regulated by two main biological mechanisms. The first is the circadian rhythm, an internal clock that operates on a roughly twenty-four-hour cycle and is primarily influenced by light exposure. When light enters the eyes, it signals the brain's suprachiasmatic nucleus to suppress the production of melatonin, a hormone that promotes sleepiness. As darkness falls, melatonin levels rise, preparing the body for sleep. The second mechanism is sleep pressure, which builds up throughout the day as a chemical called adenosine accumulates in the brain. The longer we stay awake, the stronger this sleep pressure becomes.

Sleep itself consists of several distinct stages that cycle throughout the night. The first stage is light sleep, lasting only a few minutes, during which the body begins to relax and brain waves start to slow. The second stage is deeper sleep, characterized by sleep spindles and K-complexes — bursts of brain activity that help consolidate memories and protect the brain from external disturbances. Stages three and four are collectively known as deep sleep or slow-wave sleep, which is the most restorative phase. During deep sleep, the body repairs tissues, strengthens the immune system, and releases growth hormones. The final stage is REM sleep, or rapid eye movement sleep, which is when most dreaming occurs. During REM sleep, the brain is highly active, almost as active as when we are awake, but the body's muscles are temporarily paralysed to prevent us from acting out our dreams. REM sleep plays a crucial role in emotional regulation and creative problem-solving.

The consequences of insufficient sleep are far-reaching and well-documented. Studies have shown that sleeping fewer than six hours per night on a regular basis increases the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and weakened immune function. In terms of cognitive performance, even one night of poor sleep can reduce attention span, impair decision-making, and decrease reaction time by as much as 300 percent. Drowsy driving, for example, is responsible for an estimated 20 percent of all road traffic accidents. Chronic sleep deprivation has also been linked to mental health conditions including depression and anxiety, with research suggesting that the relationship is bidirectional — poor sleep worsens mental health, and mental health difficulties disrupt sleep.

Modern lifestyles present numerous challenges to healthy sleep. The widespread use of electronic devices before bedtime exposes people to blue light, which suppresses melatonin production and delays the onset of sleep. Caffeine, which has a half-life of approximately five to six hours, consumed even in the early afternoon can significantly impair sleep quality later that night. Shift work, jet lag, and irregular schedules disrupt the circadian rhythm, leading to what researchers call social jet lag — a chronic misalignment between the body's internal clock and the demands of daily life. To improve sleep quality, experts recommend maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, creating a cool and dark sleeping environment, avoiding caffeine and alcohol in the hours before bed, and establishing a relaxing pre-sleep routine such as reading or gentle stretching.

title.en: Passage 1 - The Development of Public Libraries
title.zh: 文章1 - 公共图书馆的发展

sections.passage:
The concept of a public library — a collection of books and other materials available to all members of a community free of charge — is relatively modern in the history of human civilization. While libraries have existed for thousands of years, from the ancient Library of Alexandria to the monastic libraries of medieval Europe, these were invariably restricted to scholars, clergy, and the elite. The idea that ordinary citizens should have free access to knowledge emerged gradually during the Enlightenment and took concrete institutional form in the 19th century.

The first truly public library in the modern sense is generally considered to be the Peterborough Town Library in New Hampshire, United States, which opened in 1833 and was funded by taxation. However, the most significant early development in public library history was the Public Libraries Act of 1850 in the United Kingdom, which empowered local boroughs to establish free public libraries funded by local taxes. The act was championed by William Ewart, a Member of Parliament, and Edward Edwards, a self-taught librarian who became the first chief librarian of the Manchester Free Library when it opened in 1852. Despite initial resistance from those who objected to using public funds for such purposes, the movement grew rapidly. By 1900, there were over 300 public libraries operating across Britain.

In the United States, the public library movement received its greatest boost from the philanthropy of Andrew Carnegie, the Scottish-American steel magnate. Between 1883 and 1929, Carnegie funded the construction of 2,509 public libraries worldwide, including 1,689 in the United States and 660 in the United Kingdom and Ireland. Carnegie believed that access to books was essential for self-improvement and democratic participation, and he required recipient communities to commit to ongoing funding for staffing and book purchases as a condition of his grants. His libraries were characterised by their distinctive architecture, often featuring grand entrance halls, reading rooms with high ceilings, and ample natural light.

The 20th century saw public libraries evolve from simple book lending institutions into comprehensive community centres. Libraries began offering a wide range of services including reference collections, children's programmes, literacy classes, and access to emerging technologies. The introduction of computer terminals in the 1980s and internet access in the 1990s transformed libraries into vital digital inclusion resources, particularly for communities where home internet access was not universal. Today, many libraries offer services that would be unrecognizable to their founders, including maker spaces with 3D printers, recording studios, coding workshops, and social services referrals.

Despite their evolution, public libraries face significant challenges in the 21st century. Budget cuts have led to reduced opening hours, staff layoffs, and in some cases permanent closures. Between 2010 and 2020, the United Kingdom lost approximately 800 library branches, while the United States has seen a similar trend of consolidation and closure. Advocates argue that libraries remain essential democratic institutions that promote literacy, bridge the digital divide, and provide safe community spaces, particularly for vulnerable populations including the elderly, homeless individuals, and new immigrants. The debate over the future of public libraries reflects broader questions about the role of public services in an increasingly digital world.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Employment
title.zh: 文章2 - 人工智能对就业的影响

sections.passage:
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technology has sparked intense debate about its impact on employment and the future of work. While previous waves of automation primarily affected manual labour and routine manufacturing tasks, modern AI systems are increasingly capable of performing cognitive tasks that were once considered the exclusive domain of human intelligence, including language translation, medical diagnosis, legal document analysis, and even creative writing. This has led to growing concern that AI could displace workers on an unprecedented scale.

A landmark 2013 study by Frey and Osborne at Oxford University estimated that 47 percent of total US employment was at high risk of automation within the following two decades. The study analysed 702 occupations and classified them according to their probability of computerisation, finding that jobs involving routine cognitive tasks — such as bookkeeping, data entry, and basic customer service — were most vulnerable. However, jobs requiring social intelligence, creative thinking, and complex problem-solving were found to be significantly less susceptible to automation. Professions such as nursing, teaching, and counselling, which require empathy and nuanced human interaction, were among the least likely to be replaced.

Subsequent research has offered more nuanced perspectives. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development published a report in 2019 suggesting that while 14 percent of jobs in OECD countries were highly automatable, a further 32 percent could face significant changes in how they are performed. This distinction is important: rather than eliminating entire occupations, AI is more likely to transform the nature of work within those occupations. For example, AI tools can now assist radiologists in analysing medical scans, but most experts agree that this will augment rather than replace human expertise, allowing radiologists to process more cases with greater accuracy while focusing their clinical judgement on complex or ambiguous cases.

The historical record of technological revolutions provides both reassurance and caution. Previous waves of automation — from the spinning jenny to the assembly line to the personal computer — ultimately created more jobs than they destroyed, though the transition periods were often painful and prolonged. The key question is whether AI represents a fundamentally different kind of technological disruption. Unlike previous technologies that replaced physical tasks, AI can potentially perform a wide range of cognitive tasks across virtually all sectors simultaneously, raising the possibility that the pace of displacement could outstrip the economy's ability to generate new forms of employment.

Several strategies have been proposed to manage the transition to an AI-augmented economy. Education systems are being urged to shift their focus from knowledge transmission to the development of skills that complement AI, including critical thinking, creativity, emotional intelligence, and digital literacy. Governments are exploring policy responses including universal basic income, robot taxes, and expanded social safety nets. Some economists advocate for a shorter working week, arguing that if AI increases productivity sufficiently, the gains could be shared through reduced working hours rather than job losses. Whatever approach is adopted, the consensus among researchers is that proactive planning and investment in human capital will be essential to ensuring that the benefits of AI are broadly shared across society.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Science of Biodiversity Loss
title.zh: 文章3 - 生物多样性丧失的科学

sections.passage:
Biodiversity — the variety of life on Earth at all levels, from genes to ecosystems — is declining at a rate unprecedented in human history. The 2019 Global Assessment Report by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services concluded that approximately one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades. This loss is not merely an environmental tragedy; it poses fundamental risks to human food security, health, and economic prosperity.

The primary driver of biodiversity loss is habitat destruction, particularly the conversion of natural ecosystems for agriculture. Since 1990, an estimated 420 million hectares of forest have been lost, primarily in tropical regions. The expansion of palm oil plantations in Southeast Asia, soybean farming in South America, and cattle ranching in the Amazon have been particularly devastating. Wetlands, which serve as critical habitats for migratory birds and act as natural water filtration systems, have declined by 35 percent globally since 1970. Grasslands, mangroves, and coral reefs have experienced similarly severe degradation.

Climate change is an increasingly significant driver of biodiversity loss that interacts with and amplifies other threats. As temperatures rise, many species are forced to migrate to higher altitudes or latitudes in search of suitable conditions. However, species that cannot move fast enough, or that have nowhere to go — such as mountaintop species or polar bears dependent on sea ice — face serious risk of extinction. A study published in Nature in 2019 found that if global temperatures rise by 2 degrees Celsius, 18 percent of insect species, 16 percent of plant species, and 8 percent of vertebrate species could lose more than half of their geographic range.

The concept of ecosystem services helps to quantify the economic value of biodiversity. These services include provisioning services such as food, timber, and freshwater; regulating services such as climate regulation, flood control, and pollination; cultural services such as recreation and spiritual value; and supporting services such as nutrient cycling and soil formation. The global value of ecosystem services has been estimated at approximately 125 trillion dollars per year, a figure that dwarfs the global GDP. Pollination alone, primarily carried out by bees and other insects, contributes an estimated 235 to 577 billion dollars to global agricultural production annually.

The consequences of biodiversity loss for human health are becoming increasingly apparent. Many pharmaceutical drugs are derived from natural compounds — aspirin from willow bark, the cancer treatment taxol from the Pacific yew tree, and the antimalarial drug artemisinin from a Chinese herb. As species disappear, so too does the potential for future medical discoveries. Biodiversity loss also increases the risk of zoonotic disease emergence, as habitat destruction brings humans into closer contact with wildlife reservoirs of novel pathogens. The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the interconnection between environmental degradation and public health.

Conservation efforts have achieved notable successes, including the recovery of species such as the bald eagle, the humpback whale, and the giant panda. Protected areas now cover approximately 15 percent of the Earth's land surface and 7 percent of its oceans, though scientists argue that at least 30 percent of both should be protected to maintain essential ecosystem functions. Innovative approaches such as payment for ecosystem services, biodiversity offsets, and nature-based solutions — which use natural processes to address societal challenges such as climate change and food security — are gaining traction. However, current global spending on biodiversity conservation is estimated at 100 billion dollars per year, far short of the 700 billion dollars that experts believe is needed to reverse the decline.
